explain.say: Imagine copying a whole book by hand. It could take months! Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg in Germany built a printing press with movable metal letters. The board shows how it worked, step by step.

explain.say: Look at the first step. Gutenberg, a metalworker, made a mould to cast many identical letters from a hot mix of lead, tin and antimony. Every letter a looked exactly the same. Why would identical letters matter?

explain.say: See the lever? Ink was dabbed on, then a big screw press, like the ones for squeezing grapes, pushed paper onto the letters. One press could print hundreds of pages a day. How much faster is that than writing?

explain.say: Now the timeline. By 1500, presses in over 250 European towns had printed millions of books, and ideas spread faster than ever. Great work! Wow: Korea's Jikji, printed in 1377, is even older: the oldest surviving book printed with metal type.

faq.a: He used a hand mould to cast letters from a mix of lead, tin and antimony. The mix melted easily, cooled quickly and was hard enough to print many times.
asks: What was movable type made of?

faq.a: Printing flips the image, like a rubber stamp. So letters were set as a mirror image, and they came out the right way round on paper.
asks: Why are printing letters back to front?

faq.q: Where did the idea for the press come from?
faq.a: Gutenberg adapted screw presses already used for squeezing grapes for wine, olives for oil, and for pressing paper.
asks: How did the printing press work?

faq.q: How many Gutenberg Bibles were printed?
faq.a: Probably about 180 copies around 1455, some on paper and some on vellum, which is calf skin. About 49 survive today, whole or in part.
Books became cheaper and more common, so more people learned to read. Ideas in science, religion and politics spread quickly, helping the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.
asks: Why was the printing press important?

facts: About 180 Gutenberg Bibles were printed around 1455, and 49 survive at least in part.
Jikji, printed in Korea in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
William Caxton set up England's first printing press at Westminster in 1476.
